title: Economics in Tech Policy
gist: A landing page for Oxford Economics' 'Economics in Tech Policy' series on Asia-Pacific, arguing that AI governance, digital regulation, copyright, cross-border data flows and digital infrastructure are usually debated in isolation but pose the same economic questions on investment, innovation, adoption and competitiveness. The substantive signal is thin: three published pieces are summarised in a line each (a 95-country study linking digital regulation to startup creation and VC, a case against AI self-sufficiency in APAC, and a 'dysregulation' cumulative-burden framing), with three more listed as coming soon.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues Asia-Pacific technology policies must be assessed as a cumulative stack rather than issue-by-issue, because individually well-intentioned rules on AI governance, digital regulation, copyright, data flows and infrastructure combine to shape investment, innovation and technology adoption.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Country risk models for APAC tech exposure that score regulations one at a time will understate the compounded compliance drag on capex and market entry.
insights.quote: Why technology policies need to be considered together, and how individually well-intentioned decisions can combine to shape investment, innovation and technology adoption.
insights.locator: Dysregulation and the economics of AI policy

insights.claim: The series pipeline flags AI and copyright, cross-border data flows and digital trade, and AI and digital infrastructure as the next APAC policy fights Oxford Economics expects to matter economically, all listed as 'coming soon' rather than published.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: A cheap forward calendar of where APAC regulatory headlines are likely to land for data-center, cloud and content-licensing exposure.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics uses evidence from 95 countries to link digital regulation to startup creation and venture capital investment, framing regulation in Asia as an economic growth question rather than a purely legal or consumer-protection one.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Gives VC allocators a cross-country empirical basis to discount APAC markets tightening digital rules, and to favour those that are not.
insights.quote: What evidence from 95 countries tells us about the relationship between digital regulation, startup creation and venture capital investment.
insights.locator: Why digital regulation is now an economic growth question in Asia

insights.claim: 74% of startups surveyed across India, Malaysia and South Korea report that digital regulations increase compliance-related costs, according to Oxford Economics research.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of the fixed-cost hurdle facing early-stage APAC tech, which structurally favours incumbents with existing compliance functions.
insights.quote: 74% of startups across India, Malaysia, and South Korea, report that digital regulations increase compliance- related costs
insights.locator: Digital regulations and the startup ecosystem in Asia

insights.claim: Oxford Economics contends that pursuing AI sovereignty through greater self-sufficiency would hold the Asia-Pacific back, costing investment, innovation and access to global AI capabilities.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Cuts against the prevailing national-champion AI narrative; a lever for global hyperscalers and chip suppliers arguing against localisation mandates in APAC procurement.
insights.quote: Why pursuing AI sovereignty through greater self-sufficiency can come at a cost to investment, innovation and access to global AI capabilities.
insights.locator: Why full AI self-sufficiency would hold Asia Pacific back

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' sovereign AI research was commissioned by the AI Adoption Initiative, an industry-facing sponsor whose interests align with the report's pro-openness conclusion.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Sponsorship context to weigh before citing the sovereign-AI findings as independent evidence in policy or investment memos.
insights.quote: Oxford Economics was commissioned by the AI Adoption Initiative to develop a research report
insights.locator: The economics of sovereign AI: balancing autonomy

themes.theme: Asia's policy assertiveness as a business variable

insights.claim: Oxford Economics positions government affairs as a strategically rising function in Asia, describing a new era of policy assertiveness in which policy, not just growth, drives business outcomes for international firms.
insights.speaker: Anusha Suthenthiran
insights.so_what: Suggests rising regulatory beta in APAC earnings for multinationals; policy capability becomes a differentiator worth underwriting alongside demand growth.
insights.quote: Asia remains one of the world’s most dynamic growth regions—but the forces shaping business outcomes are changing.
